title: Give, then never bring it up again.
subtitle: The gift that is not followed by reminders

row.title: the moment I hand it over

then: Ibn Kathir: Allah praises those who give and then {trap}do not remind the receiver, by word or action{/trap}, nor harm them. Their reward is {reward}with their Lord Himself{/reward}, with no fear on the Day and no grief over what they leave behind.
now: You lent your brother money last year. Every family dinner, you drop a little hint. You paid for your friend's ticket and mention it when you argue. {trap}Each hint takes a bite out of the gift.{/trap}
old: I gave it, so I have a right to mention it now and then.
new: A gift is complete when I let it go and never use it against anyone.
try: Think of something you gave that you keep bringing up. Decide today never to mention it again.

title: A kind word and forgiveness beat charity that stings.
subtitle: When you cannot give without hurting, give words instead
then: Ibn Kathir explains the kind word as {reward}compassionate speech and a dua for Muslims{/reward}, and forgiveness as {reward}pardoning a wrong done to you{/reward}. These are better than charity followed by injury. Allah is Rich, needing nothing, and Forbearing.
now: Someone asks you for help on a day you are broke and irritated. You could throw a fiver at them with a lecture. {reward}Or you could say, I cannot today, may Allah make it easy for you, and mean it.{/reward}
old: Giving something is always better than giving nothing.
new: A gentle word or a pardon can be worth more than money given with a sting.
try: The next time you have to say no to someone asking, say it with a sincere dua for them.

title: Charity for show is dust on a rock. Rain leaves it bare.
subtitle: How reminders and showing off erase a deed

key.label: What it looked like vs what it was

then: Ibn Kathir describes the show-off who {trap}pretends to give for Allah but seeks people's praise{/trap}. His deeds are like dust on a smooth rock: they look plentiful, then {trap}a downpour leaves it bare{/trap}. Ad-Dahhak said the parable also fits the one who gives and then reminds or harms.
now: The donation screenshot posted to your story. The fundraiser where you make sure your name is read out. {trap}It looks like a lot of dust on the rock.{/trap} Ask yourself who the gift was really for.
old: As long as the money reaches the needy, my motive does not matter.
new: If I give to be seen, the rain can wash away everything I thought I had.
try: Give one gift this week that nobody, not even your closest friend, will know about.

title: Sincere giving is a hilltop garden. Even a drizzle makes it fruit.
subtitle: The opposite of dust on a rock
then: Right after the bare rock comes the garden. Those who give {idea}seeking only Allah's pleasure, certain He will reward them{/idea}, are like a garden on a height. Ibn Kathir says {reward}if heavy rain does not fall, light rain suffices{/reward}: the believer's good deeds never become barren.
now: You only have a little to give this month, a coin in the box, a sandwich for the man at the station. {reward}With sincerity, that drizzle is enough.{/reward} Allah sees what you do.
old: My small gifts are too little to matter.
new: Given sincerely, even a small gift falls on fertile ground and grows.
try: Give something small today and quietly say: for You, Allah.

title: A lifetime garden burned just when he was old and needed it.
subtitle: Do not undo your good deeds at the end
then: Umar asked the Companions who this verse was about; they said Allah knows best. Young Ibn Abbas spoke up: {idea}it is a parable for a deed{/idea}, a man who did good, then {trap}turned to disobedience until he annulled his good works{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ used to pray: make Your widest provision for me in my old age.
now: Years of volunteering, then a bitter falling-out that turns into slander. A lifetime of prayer, then a business deal that cheats people. {trap}A good garden can burn late.{/trap} Protect what you built.
old: I have done enough good in my life; I am set.
new: My good deeds are a garden I must keep guarding until my last day.
try: Make the Prophet's ﷺ dua today: O Allah, make Your widest provision for me in my old age.

title: Do not give Allah what you would only take with eyes closed.
subtitle: Giving from the best, not the leftovers
then: Al-Bara said the Ansar would {reward}hang date branches in the Prophet's masjid ﷺ for the poor emigrants{/reward}. Some {trap}slipped in poor dates among the good{/trap}. Ibn Abbas said: how do you accept for Me what you would not accept for yourselves? Allah is Rich and Praiseworthy.
now: Clearing out your wardrobe and sending the stained shirts to the charity bag. Donating the expired tins from the back of the cupboard. {idea}Would you take it with your eyes open?{/idea}
old: Charity is a good place for the things I do not need anymore.
new: I give Allah the kind of thing I would be happy to receive myself.
try: Give away one thing in good condition that you actually like.

title: Shaytan whispers you will go broke. Allah promises forgiveness and more.
subtitle: Two voices when you reach for your wallet
then: The Prophet ﷺ said Shaytan and the angel both touch the heart. {trap}Shaytan's touch threatens evil and denies truth{/trap}; {reward}the angel's touch promises good and confirms truth{/reward}. Whoever feels the first should seek refuge in Allah. Then he recited this verse.
now: You see the appeal for the flood victims. A voice says: rent is due, you cannot afford this, be sensible. {trap}Notice where that voice comes from.{/trap} Allah's promise is forgiveness and more, not less.
old: My fear of running out is just being responsible.
new: The fear of poverty that stops all giving is a whisper, and Allah promises more.
try: Next time fear stops you from giving, say a'udhu billah and give a little anyway.

title: Whoever is given wisdom has been given a lot of good.
subtitle: The gift worth envying
then: Ibn Abbas said wisdom here is {idea}knowledge of the Qur'an{/idea}: its clear and less clear parts, what it permits and forbids, its parables. Ibn Mas'ud heard the Prophet ﷺ say {reward}no envy except in two{/reward}: a man given wealth who spends it rightly, and a man given wisdom who judges by it and teaches it.
now: You scroll past the influencer's holiday and feel a pang. {idea}The person truly worth envying is the one who understands the Qur'an and lives it.{/idea} That gift is still on offer to you.
old: The people I admire most are the ones with the best lifestyle.
new: Wisdom from Allah is the real wealth, and I can ask Him for it.
try: Spend ten minutes today reading the explanation of one verse you recite often.

title: Every coin you spend and every vow you make, Allah knows.
subtitle: Nothing given is lost or unseen
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah has {idea}perfect knowledge of every good deed, charity and vow{/idea}, and rewards greatly when it is done for His Face. Those who turn away from Him have {trap}no helpers{/trap} to save them on the Day.
now: The vow you made in the hospital corridor: if she pulls through, I will. The monthly direct debit no one knows about. {idea}Allah knows every one.{/idea} Have you kept the promise you made when you were scared?
old: Promises made in a crisis do not really count once it passes.
new: Allah knows every promise I made Him and every coin I gave.
try: Remember one promise you made to Allah in a hard moment. Take one step to keep it.
